szoveg_eredeti:
Review Finds Artificial Intelligence Improves Blast Vibration Predictions Only Under Specific Conditions

A comprehensive systematic review evaluating predictive modeling for explosive rock blasting has revealed that artificial intelligence algorithms improve the reported accuracy of ground vibration forecasts over legacy empirical equations, though this advantage remains strictly conditional rather than universal. The investigation, synthesized by Louis D. G. Tabosa and colleagues and published in Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering, critically consolidated sixty-eight primary research investigations spanning empirical, statistical, and modern machine learning methodologies. Rock blasting with confined explosive charges represents a primary, economically viable technique for rock fragmentation in mineral extraction and large civil engineering infrastructure works such as tunnels, dams, and highways. Detonating these explosive charges in boreholes generates pressures reaching gigapascals in microseconds, pulverizing nearby rock and transmitting high-amplitude seismic shock waves radially outward. As these shock waves propagate, geometric and material attenuation transform them into elastic stress waves consisting of compressional body waves, shear waves, and retrograde elliptical Rayleigh surface waves that can inflict structural damage on adjacent buildings, destabilize open-pit mine slopes, and trigger severe community disturbance.

To evaluate and mitigate this vibrational damage potential before detonation, blasting engineers rely heavily on peak particle velocity, recognized across national and international regulatory frameworks as the principal metric for structural vibration tolerance. Accurate pre-blast calculation allows site engineers to modify drilling geometries and calibrate the maximum explosive charge detonated per delay interval to keep resulting ground shaking within legal thresholds. For decades, practical engineering relied on classical empirical power-law formulations pioneered between 1959 and 1979 by the United States Bureau of Mines, Langefors and Kihlstrom, and Ambraseys and Hendron. These foundational models normalize propagation distance against explosive weight through the concept of scaled distance, typically expressing distance divided by the square root or cube root of the charge per delay. While computationally trivial and straightforward to deploy using standard field measurements, empirical equations depend entirely on site-specific regression constants that fail when transferred across disparate rock masses, ignoring influential variables such as rock jointing, weathering, compressive strength, hole spacing, and initiation sequences.

With computational expansion during the 1980s, researchers introduced multivariate linear and logarithmic regressions alongside principal component analysis to incorporate parameters such as explosive detonation velocity, bench geometry, and elastic moduli. Despite extending predictive scope, multivariate statistical formulations remained constrained by assumptions of linearity or simple linearizability, leaving them ill-equipped to capture the complex, nonlinear geomechanical interactions governing seismic attenuation. The systematic review details how the subsequent paradigm shift toward artificial intelligence addressed these limitations by discovering functional patterns directly from empirical observations without prespecifying rigid mathematical curves. Methodological frameworks examined in the sixty-eight studies include feedforward artificial neural networks, support vector regression utilizing epsilon-insensitive loss boundaries and nonlinear kernel functions, tree-based ensemble methods such as random forests and extreme gradient boosting, and deep learning architectures including convolutional and recurrent networks capable of processing raw seismic waveforms.

A rigorous quantitative consolidation of the reviewed literature demonstrated that advanced data-driven models frequently achieve reported coefficients of determination exceeding 0.90, contrasting sharply with empirical baseline fits that routinely drop below 0.75 and occasionally sink beneath 0.15 on identical datasets. Support vector regression demonstrated notable stability in noisy, small-sample regimes because its optimization objective minimizes an insensitive error tube where deviations below an operational threshold incur no penalty, relying only on a sparse subset of support vectors lying on tube margins. Similarly, gradient-boosted decision trees and random forests consistently clustered at the highest tiers of reported correlation by iteratively fitting pseudo-residuals and decorrelating trees through randomized feature subsampling.

Despite these impressive metrics, the review team established that published artificial intelligence triumphs frequently reflect methodological artifacts rather than genuine operational superiority. A mechanical audit of the sixty-seven studies documenting sample sizes revealed a pronounced small-sample bias across the field, with a median dataset size of only 102 blast records. Forty-six percent of the evaluated corpus evaluated fewer than 100 blast events, and only seven percent utilized more than 300 records. Deep neural networks and flexible tree ensembles possessing hundreds of internal parameters were routinely trained on tiny datasets of several dozen blasts, creating severe vulnerability to statistical overfitting. Moreover, reporting standards across the literature proved markedly uneven: twenty-nine percent of reviewed investigations provided no empirical baseline whatsoever, while seven reported empirical baselines weaker than 0.50, artificially inflating the apparent superiority of the proposed machine learning algorithms.

The critical analysis further exposed pervasive validation weaknesses across historical publications. Seventy-eight percent of the consolidated studies calculated their headline performance metrics using a single random train-test partition drawn from one isolated blast site. Because consecutive blasts from a single quarry or open-pit operation share underlying geology, sensor instrumentation, blasting practices, and explosive suppliers, random splitting leaks spatial and operational correlation across the partition. This internal leakage produces an optimistic measure of in-distribution calibration rather than authentic predictive generalization. Across the entire sixty-eight-study corpus, not a single research team evaluated models using leave-one-site-out validation, and only two studies employed standard cross-validation schemes. The authors caution that reported coefficients of determination represent mathematical upper bounds on performance rather than transferable accuracy, leaving the true capability of uncalibrated artificial intelligence models deployed at unfamiliar mining operations largely unverified.

Contextual synthesis across mining environments further corroborated that geological classification does not determine predictive accuracy. Stratifying the sixty-eight publications into distinct operational environments—including coal operations, metal-ore extraction, stone quarries, underground civil excavations, and multi-site pooled databases—revealed nearly identical median coefficients of determination between 0.92 and 0.95. The dispersion of accuracy within individual rock categories vastly exceeded differences between categories, indicating that reported accuracy reflects sample size, feature conditioning, and validation design rather than lithology. When data from geologically diverse sites are combined, the resulting structural heterogeneity exposes the cross-site variance that single-site training partitions consistently conceal.
